transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Aster Labs Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Aster Labs Infra), Marta Lopez (Aster Labs Security), Evan Park (Aster SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete):
Redwood walked Aster Labs through multi-region routing and failover design: policy-based routing, regional capacity awareness, and DR playbook options. Discussion covered latency SLOs, KV cache behavior on cross-region failover, batching/quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem constraints, and audit/KMS concerns. Action items included sharing design doc, running capacity sims, and scheduling a DR tabletop.

Topics: multi-region policy routing; regional capacity & load shaping; failover playbooks; KV cache warming and cold-start behavior; batching/quantization effects on tail latency; VPC/on-prem failover constraints and KMS/ audit logs; routing TTLs and sticky affinity.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on the account. Marcus, our SE, will drive most of the technical diagrams today.
[00:18] Marcus Chen: Hi all, thanks. Quick agenda: routing policies, capacity awareness per region, cache considerations (KV cache), batching/quantization tradeoffs, and then recommended DR playbooks. We'll leave time for Q&A and next steps.
[00:34] Priya Shah: Sounds good. For context, our current stack uses a EU + US primary region setup, and we may add APAC next quarter. Our biggest concern is maintaining p99 < 300ms for short chat prompts while avoiding cost blowups.
[00:50] Tom Reynolds: Also worth noting we run a lot of tight latency-sensitive inference for real-time user flows, but we have batch offline scoring too. We use VPC peering today for some services.
[01:06] Marcus Chen: Great — that helps set expectations. I'll reference numbers as approximate. We typically see p50/p95/p99 behaviors change dramatically when KV cache is cold or when requests cross-region and miss the local prefix cache.
[01:22] Marta Lopez: Quick security note: we need KMS/HSM integration, SSO/SAML for ops, and a clear audit trail in any failover scenario. We'll be evaluating with our security controls in mind.
[01:36] Marcus Chen: Absolutely; we'll call out where KMS integrates and how audit logs are preserved across regions.
[01:45] [02:03] Marcus Chen: Okay, first slide — Policy routing model. There are three main dimensions: latency-first, cost-first, and capacity-aware.
[02:20] Marcus Chen: Latency-first routes to the lowest RTT region with available capacity; cost-first prefers cheaper regions (e.g., lower GPU cost) and may add small latency; capacity-aware uses realtime metrics to avoid routing to saturated regions. We recommend a multi-criteria policy: latency SLO + capacity buffer + regional weighting for data residency.
[02:46] Tom Reynolds: How do you define "available capacity" in that policy? Is it absolute GPU slots, queue length, or modeled latency?
[02:56] Marcus Chen: Good question. We use a combination: reported free slots (reserved/dedicated capacity), queue depth, and a queue-to-latency model that maps current queue to expected p95/p99. For Hosted customers, Redwood exports metrics per-region and per-pool; for Dedicated/Private, similar telemetry is available via the console/metrics endpoint.
[03:20] Priya Shah: If a region is near capacity, do you allow burst overflow to another region automatically? Concern is stateful pieces like KV cache — will cross-region overflow cause big cold-cache penalties?
[03:35] Marcus Chen: Yes, you can configure overflow behavior. We offer two modes: hard-failover (reject) or soft-overflow (route to next region). Soft-overflow has cache penalty — KV prefix cache and KV cache (K v) won't be warm in the target region unless you pre-warm or replicate keys. For chat-like workloads, cold KV cache can add 50–200ms depending on sequence lengths and whether the model re-computes prefixes.
[03:59] Evan Park: Do you support active replication of KV cache across regions to reduce miss impact? That sounds expensive but useful for strict SLOs.
[04:10] Marcus Chen: We do support configurable KV cache replication for Dedicated/Private deployments. Options: synchronous replication (higher cost, increased write latency), async replication with eventual consistency (lower cost, still reduces misses), or warming via tracing/popular prefixes. Many customers use a hybrid: replicate hot keys, use async for the rest. We also provide hints to seed caches during cold-starts.
[04:35] Marta Lopez: From a security standpoint, if KV cache replicates across regions, how do you handle encryption at rest and key material residency?
[04:45] Marcus Chen: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or customer HSM). You can control which KMS is used per region so key material can remain in-region if required. Audit logs mark replication events. We can also limit replication for sensitive keys.
[04:59] [05:20] Marcus Chen: Next, routing TTLs and sticky affinity. For low-latency sessions we recommend sticky sessions for the duration of the user session so the KV cache stays warm in that region — but if user moves regions, you get tradeoffs. Sticky policy options: session-ttl (minutes), token-based affinity, or per-route affinity.
[05:38] Priya Shah: Our user sessions can last 10–20 minutes often. Would a 20-minute sticky TTL help keep p99 low?
[05:46] Marcus Chen: Yes, in most cases a session TTL equal to average session length preserves cache affinity and keeps tail latency down. However you need to balance against regional capacity fragmentation: too much stickiness can overcommit a region. We typically recommend session TTL + global capacity rebalancing every 5–10 minutes.
[06:04] Tom Reynolds: About failover — what's a recommended DR playbook? We need something concrete to put in our runbooks.
[06:12] Marcus Chen: We propose a 3-step playbook: 1) Detect: aggregated region availability and SLO health from metrics and synthetic checks; 2) Failover: policy-enforced routing switch — either auto-failover to warm pool or staged failover with traffic ramp; 3) Recover: rehydrate caches and check model correctness and golden prompts.
[06:35] Marcus Chen: In auto-failover we have two modes — fast cutover (for complete region outage) and graceful ramp (for degraded capacity). Fast cutover routes traffic elsewhere immediately but expects cold cache hits; graceful ramp shifts % traffic over time to avoid huge cold-cache surges.
[06:53] Priya Shah: For the graceful ramp, how do you recommend we size cross-region batch windows and warming to avoid p99 spikes?
[07:03] Marcus Chen: Use controlled ramping with parallel cache warming. Steps: 1) start with 10% overflow; 2) warm top N prefixes async; 3) monitor p95/p99; 4) increment by 10% every minute if health is stable. Also increase batching slightly during the ramp to amortize overhead if your workload tolerates a few 10s ms extra latency. Batching helps throughput but can worsen tail latency if not tuned.
[07:32] Evan Park: That last point — increasing batching during failover — is counterintuitive: doesn't batching add latency for individual requests?
[07:41] Marcus Chen: It does add queueing latency for single requests, but increases throughput and reduces per-token cost. For a short failover period, we often use micro-batching (2–4 reqs) to smooth latency spikes for the fleet and to reduce CPU/GPU kernel thrash. You must measure; small batches can be net beneficial during heavy cold-cache churn.
[08:02] [08:20] Tom Reynolds: How about quantization? Some of our models are quantized in prod — does routing to a region with a different quantized runtime cause quality regressions?
[08:30] Marcus Chen: We surface model-compatibility in the catalog. If you route to a region with a variant (e.g., Q4, 4-bit or int8), you can set fallbacks: allow only compatible variants or transcode on the fly (which is expensive). Usually we advise pinning model families per-region or using a quality threshold: if the fallback model's eval score on a canonical prompt set is within acceptable delta, route; else reject or log and notify.
[08:58] Priya Shah: We have strict quality requirements on some prompts — can we tag certain routes as "quality-critical" so they never overflow to quantized variants?
[09:07] Marcus Chen: Yes; per-route policy tags support that. You tag routes "quality-critical" and policy routing enforces model-family and quantization constraints. Those routes will either queue or fail if the preferred region lacks capacity.
[09:20] Marta Lopez: From a compliance standpoint we also need audit trails showing which region served a request and any KMS key used. Do you log that?
[09:29] Marcus Chen: Yes — per-request metadata includes region, instance id, model variant, KMS key id, and policy decision reason. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM or shipped to S3 with retention policies.
[09:44] [10:03] Marcus Chen: Now, some real-world numbers we've seen: cross-region cold KV miss penalty ~50–200ms depending on model and sequence length. Warm local cache can yield p99 as low as 150–300ms for short prompts; cross-region without replication can push p99 > 500ms for some workloads. These are rough but helpful to budget.
[10:26] Priya Shah: That aligns with our observations. Our p95 is usually fine, but p99 spikes during peak traffic — likely cold cache + queueing.
[10:35] Marcus Chen: Right, p99 is sensitive. One mitigation is proactive cache seeding and synthetic traffic on key prefixes during peak hours. Another is preserving affinity for heavy users.
[10:47] Tom Reynolds: On the telemetry side, what metrics should we export to our monitoring so we can run automated failover?
[10:55] Marcus Chen: Recommended metrics: per-region free_slots, queue_depth, p95/p99 latency, synthetic-check success rate, model-health checks (real-time evals), and KV cache hit ratio. We emit those as Prometheus metrics or push to an endpoint.
[11:11] Evan Park: What about multi-region DNS vs global load balancer vs client SDK routing — which one does Redwood recommend?
[11:20] Marcus Chen: We support multiple deployment patterns: 1) Client-side SDK routing with policy decisioning (best control, reduces wide-net routing), 2) Global LB with edge-aware steering (simple), 3) DNS-based routing (coarser). For low-latency apps, client-side or edge steering is better because you can make per-request policy decisions and attach session affinity tokens.
[11:44] Priya Shah: Our frontend is largely browser-based. Client-side routing might leak region endpoints. Any privacy/regulatory concern?
[11:54] Marcus Chen: If exposure of region endpoints is a concern, use an edge proxy/ingress that implements the policy, so client talks to a regional gateway and the gateway does regional decisions. That keeps endpoints internal.
[12:07] [12:30] Marcus Chen: Now, VPC/on-prem constraints. For Private deployments, network egress and limited peering can make cross-region failover slower. If you have an on-prem region, you can set a separate failover window because network path retear/peering adjustments can take longer.
[12:50] Tom Reynolds: For our VPC peered setup, any recommendations for keeping failover fast without violating our security posture?
[12:58] Marcus Chen: Use static peering + pre-provisioned NAT/EGW routes, and test path failover regularly. Keep a warm standby in another region with pre-shared keys and HSM access. Also, use certificate pinning and automations for route table updates.
[13:18] Marta Lopez: For HSM/KMS, if we restrict keys to region, does that prevent you from decrypting caches in another region during failover?
[13:27] Marcus Chen: If keys are region-locked, you cannot decrypt remote caches. For strict residency you must accept cache cold-misses during failover, or you can use an approved pattern: replicate encrypted artifacts and decrypt only with the region's key after failover, but that presumes key policy allows it. We can show you patterns used with customers who have strict control.
[13:46] [14:05] Priya Shah: Something about model warmup: does Redwood provide tooling to pre-warm model KV caches when we scale up a region or bring up capacity?
[14:13] Marcus Chen: Yes — there are warmup APIs and replay utilities. You can supply a set of canonical prompts to pre-populate KV caches. For Dedicated you can also snapshot and ship a cache image between regions, though snapshotting is eventually consistent and has size constraints.
[14:29] Tom Reynolds: Snapshotting cache images sounds helpful — is it incremental?
[14:34] Marcus Chen: We support incremental snapshots for hot key sets and full snapshots for smaller models. Incrementals are recommended for large-scale systems to reduce bandwidth and time.
[14:44] [15:00] Marcus Chen: Now let's cover an example DR scenario: Region A full outage at 16:00. Auto-detect triggers: synthetic checks fail + p99>1000ms. Auto-failover (fast cutover) routes traffic to Region B. Expected immediate effect: traffic spike in Region B queue -> cold-cache hits -> p99 spikes for first 5–15 minutes. If you have async-replication and pre-warm scripts running, the tail returns to normal after 10–30 minutes.
[15:32] Priya Shah: For our user-facing sessions, 10–30 minutes of degraded p99 is bad. How can we reduce that?
[15:40] Marcus Chen: Options: 1) Synchronous replication of hot KV keys (reduces time to recovery), 2) Pre-warm hot prefixes on failover with parallel workers, 3) Keep a small replicated warm pool in standby region for critical routes (costly but lowest latency impact).
[16:00] Tom Reynolds: Cost question — synchronous replication sounds expensive. Do you have ballpark multipliers?
[16:07] Marcus Chen: Roughly synchronous replication increases network and storage costs and may add 5–20% write latency depending on distance; overall cost depends on cache size and write rate. Many customers prefer async + hot-key replication for a middle ground.
[16:24] [16:40] Marcus Chen: Aster — if you have strict p99 for a subset of routes, we recommend a split strategy: dedicated warm standby for those routes, async replication for the rest. That gives you a cheap bulk + guaranteed low-latency for critical paths.
[16:58] Marta Lopez: How would REMOTE logging of audit events behave during a failover? Do events get buffered?
[17:07] Marcus Chen: Logs are buffered locally with guaranteed-at-least-once delivery to your configured sink. We also tag events with pre- and post-failover region metadata. If a sink is unreachable, they are queued and shipped when connectivity returns. For extremely high compliance, we can enable triple-write to multiple sinks.
[17:27] Evan Park: Are there any recommended chaos testing scenarios we should run to validate the playbook?
[17:34] Marcus Chen: Yes — do a series: 1) regional outage (kill region), 2) partial degradation (simulate high queue depth), 3) KMS failure (region key unavailable), 4) network partition between regions, 5) cache corruption scenario. For each, verify failover triggers, observe p95/p99, and validate audit logs and rollback. We can help run guided chaos drills.
[18:03] Priya Shah: Can Redwood run simulated traffic from our production traces to validate the plan?
[18:10] Marcus Chen: We can — with redacted traces or synthetic traffic. We also have a capacity spreadsheet where you input qps, average tokens, and model variant and we estimate throughput/latency and expected cross-region impact. We'll share that.
[18:27] [18:45] Tom Reynolds: On the matter of routing decisions — are they deterministic? If a request is re-routed mid-session will you preserve affinity using a token?
[18:55] Marcus Chen: We use session tokens for affinity. If mid-session re-route is necessary, we support routing the subsequent requests to a warmed replica if available, or we accept a cache miss. You can choose between sticky-only or sticky-with-override where policy overrides affinity under heavy load.
[19:14] Priya Shah: For analytics and billing, do you provide per-region token counts and a breakdown by model variant?
[19:21] Marcus Chen: Yes — per-region/per-model/ per-route billing export is available. You can export CSVs or integrate with billing APIs for deeper analysis.
[19:32] [19:50] Marcus Chen: Quick note: for Dedicated deployments, you can reserve specific GPU pools per region with burst capacity. That makes capacity-aware routing simpler because you have guaranteed slots to failover into.
[20:02] Tom Reynolds: If we reserve burst capacity, is that warm (cache warm) or cold?
[20:09] Marcus Chen: Typically cold. You can opt to keep a small warm pool running to serve heat-critical routes, but that has an ongoing cost. Warm pools do maintain cache and model weights resident.
[20:20] Marta Lopez: For our internal audit we need a DR playbook that enumerates who can trigger manual failover. Can Redwood expose RBAC controls to limit who can flip the switch?
[20:31] Marcus Chen: Yes — RBAC for failover controls exists. We integrate with SSO (SAML/OAuth) and let you gate manual failover behind a role and an approval flow. All manual actions are logged.
[20:40] [21:00] Marcus Chen: Let's go through a short example policy YAML snippet (paraphrased):
- name: "chat-low-latency"
  policy: latency-first
  affinity: session-ttl=20m
  fallback: graceful-ramp
  allowed_models: ["gptx-8b", "gptx-8b-q4"]
  quality_tag: "critical"

We can share a full doc with multiple examples.
[21:31] Priya Shah: That looks useful. We'll want a variant for "batch scoring" which is cost-first and allows quantized variants.
[21:39] Marcus Chen: Absolutely.
[21:44] [22:00] Evan Park: On monitoring, can Redwood emit alerts when policy routing begins to overflow a region? We want to know before full failover.
[22:08] Marcus Chen: Yes — you can set thresholds on queue depth or synthetic checks to trigger alerts. We also surface policy-decision traces so you can see why a request was routed.
[22:21] Tom Reynolds: How do you handle eventual consistency for async replicated caches if we fail back to original region? Is there a merge conflict problem?
[22:30] Marcus Chen: We use key versioning and last-writer-wins semantics for KV caches; for critical keys you can set a lock or use synchronous writes. When failing back, we recommend a reconcile step: verify hot keys and run consistency checks to avoid regressions.
[22:50] [23:10] Marcus Chen: A couple of operational tips: 1) keep a compact list of golden prompts for each route so you can smoke-test quality post-failover, 2) schedule periodic cache snapshots for critical routes, 3) document which model variants are allowed per-region in the policy.
[23:32] Priya Shah: Regarding smoke tests, can we automate a daily synthetic check per-region with our golden prompts?
[23:41] Marcus Chen: Yes — Redwood supports scheduled synthetic checks and you can plug them into alerting.
[23:49] [24:10] Priya Shah: A security question — what happens to encryption keys during a region failover if our KMS provider is temporarily unreachable?
[24:20] Marcus Chen: If KMS is unreachable in a region you'll either block decryption (if keys are region-locked) or use a fallback policy if you permitted cross-region key access. You can configure a fail-open (not recommended) or fail-close policy. For compliance we usually advise fail-close.
[24:38] Marta Lopez: We'll probably choose fail-close for most sensitive routes.
[24:44] [25:05] Marcus Chen: Onboarding checklist for multi-region: 1) define route categories (critical vs cost), 2) select replication strategy for KV cache, 3) choose failover mode per route, 4) set TTLs and affinity, 5) set up monitoring/alerts, 6) run chaos tests. We'll send this checklist.
[25:28] Tom Reynolds: Can you provide the capacity spreadsheet now? Even a sample so we can plug in numbers.
[25:34] Marcus Chen: We'll attach a template. It takes qps, avg tokens, percent heavy sessions and outputs estimated GPU count and expected p95/p99 with different cache scenarios.
[25:47] [26:05] Priya Shah: One practical operational question: during failover can we prefer certain AZs in a region because some AZs have lower latency to our CDN PoPs?
[26:15] Marcus Chen: Yes — you can add AZ / instance affinity into the policy, though that makes scheduling and autoscaling constraints more complex. It's doable if you document preferred AZs.
[26:29] Evan Park: For private deployments, are there any limits on cross-region replication due to NAT & firewall rules?
[26:37] Marcus Chen: You may need to open specific egress ports and authorize peers. We provide a network appendix with required endpoints and ports; some customers set up a dedicated replication VPC peering for cache replication traffic.
[26:52] [27:10] Marcus Chen: A quick note on observability: we recommend instrumenting request-level tags: route_id, session_id, region_shard, policy_reason. That allows you to pivot quickly when investigating spikes.
[27:24] Priya Shah: We'll need that for our SRE runbooks.
[27:28] [27:45] Tom Reynolds: Are there licensing/contract nuances for Dedicated multi-region deployments? For example, support for warm standby in multiple regions — is that an add-on?
[27:55] Lena Ortiz: Yes typically reserved standby capacity is priced differently. We'll include pricing estimates in the follow-up and map to your expected QPS.
[28:06] [28:20] Marcus Chen: Final technical point — latency budgets should explicitly account for cache miss penalties and cross-region network RTT. For example, if your p99 SLO is 300ms and cross-region RTT is 120ms, you must ensure local processing is under 180ms ideally.
[28:39] Priya Shah: That math helps. We'll run numbers against our prompts.
[28:44] [29:00] Marcus Chen: Okay let's capture the explicit next steps. (summarizing) Lena will share the multi-region routing doc and policy examples; Marcus will share capacity spreadsheet and recommended chaos tests; Aster will share regional traffic mix and set DR tabletop date; Redwood to prepare security whitepaper + SOC2 artifacts.
[29:22] Lena Ortiz: I'll also include a short example playbook YAML and a sample failover checklist in the doc.
[29:30] Evan Park: Good. Also please include a sample of warmup scripts for KV prefix seeding.
[29:38] Marcus Chen: We'll include that.
[29:42] [30:00] Priya Shah: A quick question about billing attribution during failover — will tokens served in fallback regions be billed to our account as normal, and will we get region-labeled usage?
[30:11] Lena Ortiz: Yes, billed as normal with per-region breakdowns. We'll note any extra charges for replication or warm standby.
[30:22] Marta Lopez: One last security ask: can you provide an example of the audit trail showing region decision + KMS key id per request? We need to validate with our compliance team.
[30:32] Marcus Chen: We'll include a redacted sample log entry in the security pack.
[30:38] [31:00] Tom Reynolds: Might be worth a brief run-through of a live scenario next week — perhaps a focused session on chaos testing. Can we schedule that in the follow-up?
[31:09] Lena Ortiz: Yes — propose a 90-minute guided drill for the team. We'll coordinate dates.
[31:16] [31:40] Priya Shah: Thanks. On the engineering side, we'll prepare traffic numbers and list of golden prompts.
[31:47] Marcus Chen: Great. Any other deep technical questions before we wrap?
[31:54] Priya Shah: One: how do you handle model rollout compatibility across regions during staged rollouts? Say we deploy a new model in Region A first.
[32:04] Marcus Chen: Use rollout policies: canary by percent, region-scoped rollouts, and automatic rollback on metric regression. You can pin traffic for critical routes until eval passes. We also support shadow testing to validate model outputs without serving to users.
[32:20] Tom Reynolds: Does shadowing create KV cache pollution?
[32:24] Marcus Chen: We run shadow traffic in readonly mode for model runs to avoid polluting shared KV caches, or we scope cache namespaces per rollout.
[32:33] [33:00] Marcus Chen: A quick note about model artifacts — moving a model variant between regions can take minutes to tens of minutes depending on size and if you warm it. We usually pre-pull heavy models into standby regions if you need fast failover.
[33:17] Priya Shah: We'll need to enumerate which models require that.
[33:22] [33:40] Marcus Chen: Alright, wrapping up. We'll put everything in a follow-up package: design doc, playbook, capacity sheet, security pack, and warmup scripts.
[33:52] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with dates for the DR tabletop and the chaos drill.
[34:00] Priya Shah: Thanks. Appreciate the thoroughness.
